[CHARACTERS: Lirael:F, Julian:M]

[TITLE: "Veil of Misalignment"]

[SYNOPSIS: In the Veilwood clearing, Lirael supervises a youth's First Sacrifice under the council's gaze. When the wish twists toward her own hidden lineage, the price of intervention threatens her standing and safety. Can she maintain the facade as the assembly draws its conclusions?]

The youth's voice rose steady through the veil-canopy, reciting the rehearsed lines about discipline and training. I stood sealed at the center, the gossamer band drawn tight across my mouth, the ornamented sash heavy on my sheer tunic. Two dozen First Favored watched from the crimson spiralgrass, their Weave-Script shifting in quiet expectation.

Julian waited at the edge, his slate-blue skin luminous, silver patterns drifting across his shoulders. A single leaf clung to the cuff of his sleeve, trembling each time he exhaled. My fingers found the silver cufflink and twisted it tighter, the chain shortening under my thumb.

The youth finished the opening invocation. Relief loosened my shoulders for one breath. Then she looked straight at me.

"I wish Lirael to find the father who left her."

The prepared sacrifice no longer matched the desire. The misalignment rang through the clearing like a wrong note. Every First Favored present felt it. The Dohkar's hands lifted. Whispers died.

I tore the gossamer band free. My voice came out hoarse. "Stop."

The twist answered before anyone could move. A figure stepped from the trees, wearing the face of the man I had described once in private, yet his eyes held no recognition of me. The youth cried out as something left her, her coral hair dimming at the roots while the figure turned away.

The assembly stared. They had seen me move. They had heard the wish name me. The inference settled on every face.

<<MICRO_EXPRESSION>>
Say it plainly — or let it show without words?
<<CONTINUE>>

Julian's left boot sole rasped once against the root beneath him as he watched the figure retreat. The youth sank to her knees, one hand pressed to her throat where the color had already begun to fade.

Do I stay and name the lineage before they ask, or slip from the clearing while their eyes are still on the twisted gift?

My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I didn't remember bringing it. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.
